title: Netflix Docuseries ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Is a Tragic, Mournful Portrait of Addiction: TV Review
description: There are not a lot of famous people in “The One About Matthew Perry.” None of the late actor’s “Friends” castmates sat for an interview for the th
body:
There are not a lot of famous people in “The One About Matthew Perry.” None of the late actor’s “Friends” castmates sat for an interview for the three-part Netflix docuseries; neither did Perry’s longtime friend and “Simpsons” star Hank Azaria, who knew Perry as a striving young actor in L.A., or later collaborators like Bradley Whitford and Aaron Sorkin.

	One could take this notable absence as an indicator of the access director Mary Robertson (“Quiet on Set”) and her team were, or were not, able to secure. But whether a matter of intention or circumstance, what emerges in place of star power is a more intimate portrait of Perry and his decadeslong struggle with substance abuse, leading to his death from a ketamine overdose in the fall of 2023. Through friends, family, fellow addicts and former partners, what emerges is a straightforwardly told, crushingly sad story of a man whose talent, humor and success were not enough to overcome a chronic disease.
	

	The unofficial protagonist of “The One About Matthew Perry” is Perry’s younger half-sister Mia Perry Bowick, a therapist who narrates what it’s like to share a loved one with the world at the peak of the monoculture. Bowick is joined by Perry’s close friends Roger Castillo and David Pressman, who recall frequent pre-fame nights with Perry and Azaria at West Hollywood’s Formosa Cafe, as well as multiple ex-girlfriends and even a member of Gen Z who met Perry in one of his many rehab stints. (She says they partly bonded because, not in spite, of their age gap: “I was born in 1997; you’re not that big a deal to me.”) Some of these voices, like “The Whole Nine Yards” director Jonathan Lynn, can speak to Perry’s artistic ability. Most, however, are there to testify to what the public didn’t see, at least until Perry chose to share his start-and-stop road to recovery in venues like his 2022 memoir.
	

	Because of such late-in-life disclosures, which Perry made after embracing his platform’s potential to help others with similar issues, there aren’t any bombshell revelations in “The One About Matthew Perry,” or even much new information. An introductory title card positions the series as “the story of Matthew Perry’s life, as told by his family and friends — and by Matthew himself.” Though recent events made me read that last clause and fear AI-assisted necromancy, Robertson’s approach is formally straightforward and free of such ill-advised techniques. Interviews are supplemented with archival clips of Perry’s screen work and interviews, and some of the show’s most searing material is conveyed in the actor’s own (previously recorded and publicized) voice.

	“God, you can do anything you want to me; just please make me famous,” Perry freely admits to praying in his youth. (He got “Friends” shortly afterward, but ruefully notes that “God didn’t forget” about the first part.) “The One About Matthew Perry” is more a collation of established facts about Perry’s battles, including a sepsis-induced coma in 2018 resulting from his use of opiates, and an unveiling of new ones. What the project adds are personal testimonies about witnessing said battles up close, plus memorable observations like “intimacy was his greatest fear and his greatest wish.” Though the most memorable lines — “Reality is an acquired taste,” say — fittingly belong to Perry.

	“Friends” has a couple of representatives in Robertson’s cast of talking heads, namely writer Jeff Strauss and former NBC Entertainment president Warren Littlefield; it wouldn’t be possible to tell Perry’s story without dwelling on his most famous role. What “The One About Matthew Perry” does is situate the sitcom’s run, which concludes by the docuseries’ halfway point, within Perry’s broader life: after a childhood feeling adrift between his remarried parents’ respective family units, before attempted follow-ups like “Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip” and addiction interfering with his work. The 2021 “Friends” reunion is presented as a source of great anxiety for Perry, who was hurt by online comments picking apart his mannerisms and appearance. Unbeknownst to viewers at the time, he was still recovering from his coma and the attendant complications.
	

	The series’ length allows “The One About Matthew Perry” to communicate the protracted, start-and-stop nature of Perry’s addiction, from first taking prescribed painkillers after an on-set injury while filming the 1997 film “Fools Rush In” to the many cycles of relapse, detox and sobriety. Eventually, the actual circumstances of Perry’s death — which resulted in multiple criminal convictions for Perry’s dealers and live-in assistant Kenneth Iwamasa, who administered the fatal drug dose — are quickly addressed in the show’s closing minutes. After so much emotion, the detour into factual legal territory via interviews with a former U.S. Attorney is abrupt, if necessary. Bowick grounds these data points with an impassioned condemnation of Iwamasa’s enabling, arguing that he should’ve tipped off family members to Perry’s ketamine abuse. Such is the function of “The One About Matthew Perry”: well-known headlines, reframed through the lesser-known perspective of those deeply affected.

	All three episodes of “The One About Matthew Perry” are now streaming on Netflix.

schema.headline: Netflix Docuseries ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Is a Tragic, Mournful Portrait of Addiction: TV Review

title: ‘Tokyo Vice’ Producer, Netflix Executive Urge Changes to Japan’s Production Incentive at MPA Seminar as Government Readies Unified Content Body
description: “Tokyo Vice” producer Alex Boden and Netflix production policy director Deb Richards urged changes to Japan’s international production incentive at
body:
“Tokyo Vice” producer Alex Boden and Netflix production policy director Deb Richards urged changes to Japan’s international production incentive at the Motion Picture Association’s annual seminar at the Tokyo International Film Festival, as the government prepares a new body to bring its scattered content-industry support under one roof.

	Boden, the London-based producer who spent almost two years in Japan making two seasons of HBO Max’s “Tokyo Vice,” traced the scheme from a 2020 research program, which “Tokyo Vice” supported, to the 2023 J-LOD incentive and today’s IP360, which offers 50% against Japanese spend.
	

	He said the minimum spend, raised to JPY800 million ($5.1 million), shut out independent films and co-productions, since most Japanese films cost between $1.5 million and $3 million. He also called for an automatic approval system in place of panel-based selection, which he said made Japan one of the few territories with a subjective incentive, at a time when projects can take three to five years to come together.

	“So how does a producer know that they can count on the Japan incentive in advance? That’s the question, and we need a solution,” Boden said. He pointed to Martin Scorsese’s “Silence,” “Pachinko” and “Shōgun” as Japan-set projects that scouted in the country but shot elsewhere, and argued for building training into the incentive, citing the U.K.’s 0.5% ScreenSkills levy as a model.

	“You can have a lower incentive, that’s fine, as long as it’s certain, as long as the criteria are clear,” Richards said during the panel. “And that’s one of the things that for the Japan incentive, the criteria is not clear.” She added that applicants could work out why they were turned down only by looking at who was approved, calling the process “opaque.”
	

	Paul Muller, the MPA’s VP of production policy for Asia-Pacific, held up Australia, where an international production must spend at least AUD20 million ($13.9 million) and put 1% of its budget toward training. Since that rule took effect in June 2023, more than AUD20 million has gone into training, he said, while the average cost of an hour of Australian TV has climbed from AUD2 million ($1.4 million) to around AUD5 million–AUD6 million ($3.5 million–$4.2 million) over seven or eight years. Muller welcomed signs that the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI), which runs the incentive, was moving from single-year to two-year financing and raising maximum thresholds.

	Georgina Pope, head of production at Toho Tombo Pictures, whose recent Japan work includes A24’s “Marty Supreme” and “Monarch: Legacy of Monsters,” said permitting in Tokyo, while still difficult, was changing. Her team recently closed the road in front of Tokyo City Hall to stage a large car scene. “I’m finding that Japan is really starting to realize the value of having a dynamic international film industry,” Pope said.

	Boden said Japan was the hottest country in the world at the moment. “Everyone seems to be in Japan or visiting Japan tomorrow,” he said, warning that letting years slip by would mean “a real missed opportunity.”

	On the government side, Nakahara Hirohiko, director-general of the Cabinet Office’s Intellectual Property Strategy Promotion Secretariat, told the seminar that a task force on the new entity held its first meeting on Oct. 22. The body, which the Japanese Prime Minister directly ordered, is meant to break down the silos between the ministries that each handle a piece of content policy: the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the Agency for Cultural Affairs, METI and, where overseas expansion is concerned, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The government aims to launch it in 2027.

	The plan forms part of a public-private investment roadmap drawn up in July, which targets JPY20 trillion ($127 billion) in overseas sales by 2033. Content is one of 17 strategic fields in the growth strategy of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s administration. For film, the roadmap covers support for luring large-scale location shoots, backing for international co-productions built on Japanese IP and tougher anti-piracy measures.
	

	“We hope to become a global hub for film shooting and production,” Nakahara said.

	Amari Akira, the former Liberal Democratic Party secretary-general and METI minister, recalled chairing the parliamentary league behind Japan’s basic content law 22 years ago, with future prime minister Kishida Fumio as its secretary-general and Hayashi Yoshimasa running its secretariat. He joked that the lineup proved his foresight. The thinking was right, he said, but execution lagged and Japan fell behind Korea in taking its content overseas.

	“In our day, we tried to do this through addition. This time, the government is doing it through multiplication,” Amari said. He described the 2033 target as a plan to quadruple the industry in 10 years and said he believed it could grow further.

	TIFF’s new festival director Hisamatsu Takeo noted that Japan was country of honor at this year’s Cannes Film Market and that 37 Japanese films screened at the recent Busan International Film Festival.

	Looking 10 years ahead, Muller said that if the government delivered on the changes discussed, the JPY20 trillion IP360 goal was “well within scope and well achievable.”

schema.headline: ‘Tokyo Vice’ Producer, Netflix Executive Urge Changes to Japan’s Production Incentive at MPA Seminar as Government Readies Unified Content Body

title: ‘Mirzapur’ Tops a Decade of Indian Streaming as New Commissions Fall, IMDb Report Finds (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Viewer interest in Indian shows on IMDb rose about 17-fold over the past decade, even as the number of new shows and seasons commissioned in the co
body:
Viewer interest in Indian shows on IMDb rose about 17-fold over the past decade, even as the number of new shows and seasons commissioned in the country has dropped for two straight years, according to a new IMDb study that traces the growth of Indian streaming through its most popular titles.

	“10 Years of Streaming in India – An IMDb Report 2026” draws on page views from the more than 250 million people who visit IMDb worldwide each month. It ranks each year’s 10 biggest Indian series from 2016 to 2026, a total of 110 slots filled by 64 different shows. It also looks past the top tier at how viewing habits and production patterns have shifted, including the rise of streaming franchises.
	

	“Mirzapur” led the pack with nine appearances, having made the list every year since it launched. “Scam 1992” was the only show to chart five times off a single season.

	Crime and thriller titles took 48 of the 110 positions. In the later years, horror, romance, comedy and drama all made gains.

	Among streamers, Prime Video and Amazon MX Player combined for 34 positions across 17 series, more than any other service. Netflix logged 21 positions spread over 18 series, the broadest range of distinct titles of the platforms the report examined.

	YouTube emerged as a launchpad. Thirteen of the 64 charting series started life there, and 11 of those were later picked up by subscription services. The report credited the platform with giving a wide base of creators room to build stories that can travel to bigger audiences.

	The Viral Fever (TVF) stood out on the production side. The company was behind nine of the charting series and 17 of the Top 10 slots, close to one in every six entries, a run that opened with “TVF Pitchers” in 2016 and reaches “Sapne vs Everyone” this year.
	

	On the talent front, the report named Pankaj Tripathi, Ali Fazal, Vikrant Massey, Jitendra Kumar, Kapil Sharma and Sunil Grover as “The MVPs of Streaming,” a group linked to recurring franchises and a string of hit series. Kay Kay Menon, Naveen Kasturia and Mona Singh ranked as the most versatile performers, each appearing in at least five series in a variety of roles rather than being anchored to one franchise. The study also pointed to multi-hyphenates such as Shahid Kapoor, Vijay Sethupathi, Samantha, Barun Sobti and Karan Tacker as examples of actors carrying an established screen persona into a new format.

	Production volume told a more cautious story. Commissions of new series and seasons hit 202 in 2023, then slipped to 169 in 2024 and 145 in 2025. The report read this as a sign of a pickier market as the business consolidates. Hindi-language shows made up 66% of Indian streaming originals in 2025.

	“Building on the success of last year’s report on Indian cinema, we turned our lens to series and used IMDb Data to understand how a decade of streaming has reshaped audience interests,” said Yaminie Patodia, head of IMDb India.

	Patodia said IMDb also brought in industry leaders to weigh in on what comes next, among them Gaurav Gandhi of Prime Video, Gunjan Soni of YouTube, Monika Shergill of Netflix, former Applause CEO Sameer Nair and Vijay Koshy of TVF.

	“Through this report, we continue to empower professionals in India with the authoritative data and insights they rely on IMDb and IMDbPro for, and to make the creative and business decisions that will shape the next decade,” Patodia said.

	IMDb is owned by Amazon.

schema.headline: ‘Mirzapur’ Tops a Decade of Indian Streaming as New Commissions Fall, IMDb Report Finds (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Tokyo Jury President Rolf de Heer on FIAPF’s New A-List: ‘It Matters a Great Deal to Some People, and Not at All to Others’
description: FIAPF’s decision to make A-list status official, with Tokyo among the 17 festivals named, is unlikely to change much about the event, according to
body:
FIAPF’s decision to make A-list status official, with Tokyo among the 17 festivals named, is unlikely to change much about the event, according to the filmmaker leading its competition jury.

	Australian filmmaker Rolf de Heer, the director of “Bad Boy Bubby” and “Ten Canoes,” was asked at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival’s jury press conference on Tuesday whether the classification mattered or was a redundant system.
	

	“I think Tokyo has always been considered one of those festivals by most people who attend festivals. Tokyo was effectively an A festival. And so in that sense, I don’t think it makes a lot of difference,” de Heer said.

	He allowed that the classification seems to be carrying more weight in determining the quality of films a festival can secure. “And so in that sense, it may help that it is officially now again A, but I don’t think it changes the festival so much,” de Heer said.

	In March, FIAPF, the international federation of film producers’ associations, replaced its four-category accreditation system with a single list and designated 17 festivals as A-list, a term the industry had long used informally. They include Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Toronto, Busan, Shanghai, Cairo and Tokyo. Busan and Toronto made the list for the first time.

	Korean producer Oh Jungwan, founder of Bom Film Productions (“The Foul King,” “A Tale of Two Sisters,” “A Bittersweet Life”), said de Heer’s answer covered it and that she was “not a film festival person.”

	“So I don’t know what is A-list or not. So maybe probably A-list means good, so but as an audience, we’re not going to the festival because of their A-list or not. We just go to watch film and enjoy the feeling, the festival feeling,” Oh said.
	

	Pressed by the journalist, who had hoped someone would call out a system that ranks some festivals above others, de Heer offered a final word: “It matters a great deal to some people, and not at all to others. And that is as it should be.”

	The rest of the jury, Japanese actor Watanabe Makiko (“M/Other,” “Love Exposure,” “Tokyo Vice”), New York- and Tokyo-based producer Alex Lo of Cinema Inutile, whose credits include Jim Jarmusch’s Venice Golden Lion winner “Father Mother Sister Brother,” and Tokyo-based colorist Yov Moor (“The Taste of Things,” “Grand Tour”), did not weigh in on the question. The five-member panel will choose the Tokyo Grand Prix from 15 competition titles. The festival runs through Nov. 4.

	De Heer was also asked about prospects for Australia-Japan co-productions. “It makes no sense for a Japanese film to shoot in Australia, it makes no sense for an Australian film to shoot in Japan. Europe is very good at doing co-productions only on a financial basis, really. Australia is not so good at that,” he said. Co-productions built on “a natural story where some things need to be shot in Japan, some things need to be shot in Australia” will always be possible, he added, “if the scripts come and if they are right.”

	Lo, whose “Heads or Tails?” won best director at Tokyo last year, said producers in Europe, the U.S. and elsewhere “are increasingly seeking co-production opportunities,” largely because local government support is lacking.

	On how a divided jury would settle on a winner, de Heer said the answer would depend on the situation. “I’m with four other very reasonable people, and I’m sure we can find a way through that we don’t end up with some sort of lesser compromised film, but a really interesting film that maybe some of us don’t like,” he said.

	Oh, a Tokyo juror for the second time, recalled once arguing for seven hours on behalf of a film. “Every other jury [member] hated me,” Oh said, adding that she hoped she would not have to fight de Heer for seven hours this time.

schema.headline: Tokyo Jury President Rolf de Heer on FIAPF’s New A-List: ‘It Matters a Great Deal to Some People, and Not at All to Others’

title: ‘Ghosts: The Possession of Button House’ Scares Up U.K., Ireland Box Office Win
description: Lionsgate U.K.’s horror-comedy “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House” debuted at the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, collecting £2.4 m
body:
Lionsgate U.K.’s horror-comedy “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House” debuted at the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, collecting £2.4 million ($3.2 million) across its opening weekend.

	Warner Bros.’ DC horror thriller “Clayface” opened in second position with $2.6 million. Amazon MGM Studios’ comedy feature “Ali G: Who Iz I?” claimed third place, generating $1.7 million in its debut session.


	Black Bear’s animated fantasy “Wildwood,” directed by Travis Knight, secured fourth spot with an opening haul of $1.36 million. Paramount’s “Street Fighter,” which led the chart in the previous session, rounded out the top five in its sophomore outing, adding $1.35 million to lift its cumulative total to $5.6 million.
	

	Universal’s animated feature “Forgotten Island” placed sixth in its second weekend, collecting $1.2 million for a cume of $3.7 million. Sony’s psychological thriller “Verity” followed in seventh position in its fourth frame, adding $857,067. The Colleen Hoover adaptation’s running total is now $14.4 million.

	Universal’s supernatural horror “Other Mommy” took eighth place in its third session with $576,822, bringing its gross to $6.2 million. Mubi’s “Fatherland” debuted at No. 9, generating $264,083 from 86 locations over the three-day frame with a sturdy $3,144 screen average – the fourth highest average per site among new releases. Including preview screenings, the drama’s total opening reached $415,017, surpassing “Cold War” to mark director Paweł Pawlikowski’s biggest-ever launch in the territory.

	Studiocanal’s animated holdover “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” rounded out the top 10 in its sixth frame, collecting $408,089 to lift its cume to $6.1 million.
	

	Meanwhile, Mubi’s documentary “Making Marie Antoinette” opened across six sites, taking $1,737 over the weekend for a $24,355 cume. The limited platform bow kicks off a staggered rollout that will expand to additional cinemas ahead of Park Circus’ re-release of Sofia Coppola’s 2006 feature “Marie Antoinette” on Nov. 13.

	Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, mid-week event programming kicks off on Tuesday with Trafalgar Releasing’s broadcast of the Royal Ballet’s “Manon,” followed on Wednesday by music documentary “Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning,” directed by Ben Wainwright-Pearce across 100+ locations.

	Wide commercial rollouts arriving on Friday across 300+ locations are led by Disney’s mountain survival documentary “Everest: The Other Side,” directed by Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin; A24’s dark comedy “Primetime,” directed by Lance Oppenheim and starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, and Phoebe Bridgers; Black Bear’s comedy “Wicker,” directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, and Elizabeth Debicki; and Kaleidoscope Entertainment’s family comedy “Arnie & Barney,” directed by Sean Heuston.

	Other releases on Friday include Universal’s comedy “I Love Boosters,” directed by Boots Riley and starring Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie, Demi Moore, and LaKeith Stanfield; Action Xtreme’s “Bad Day at the Office” across 100+ screens; Munro Films’ documentary feature “Peter Asher: Everywhere Man,” directed by Dayna Goldfine and Daniel Geller across 100+ sites; and “Pan’s Labyrinth” (20th Anniversary 4K Restoration) across 100+ locations.

	Specialized, festival, and international titles debuting Friday include BUFF Studios’ “City of Masks,” directed by Andrea M. Catinella; Picturehouse Entertainment’s “Nightborn”; Netflix’s “Gentle Monster,” directed by Marie Kreutzer and starring Léa Seydoux and Catherine Deneuve; Studiocanal’s “Animol”; and Metis Films’ “In the Shadows”. BFI Distribution is releasing a 4K restoration of Ken Russell’s classic “The Devils,” starring Vanessa Redgrave and Oliver Reed across 25+ screens, and Studiocanal is bowing the 25th anniversary 4K re-release of Richard Kelly’s “Donnie Darko,” starring Jake Gyllenhaal across 25+ locations.
	

	The weekend wraps on Saturday with Trafalgar Releasing’s event cinema presentation of “BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Sao Paulo: Live Viewing”.

schema.headline: ‘Ghosts: The Possession of Button House’ Scares Up U.K., Ireland Box Office Win

title: Donnie Iris, Pittsburgh’s Favorite Rocker, Who Scored Hits With the Jaggerz and as a Solo Artist, Dies at 83
description: Donnie Iris, regarded as Pittsburgh’s biggest hometown rock hero for a six-decade career that included hit singles in the 1960s and ’80s, died Mon
body:
Donnie Iris, regarded as Pittsburgh’s biggest hometown rock hero for a six-decade career that included hit singles in the 1960s and ’80s, died Monday at 83. He had been fighting bladder cancer for three years.

	Iris’ biggest chart success came as a member of the Jaggerz, who reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1970 with “The Rapper” — a song that dealt with “rapping” with girls, not the genre whose name had not yet been coined. 



	That group petered out, but he went on to have continued success, especially regionally, as the frontman of Donnie Iris and the Cruisers in the age of power pop and Midwest rock. A decade after “The Rapper” broke through, Iris had a hit again with “Ah! Leah!,” which reached No. 29 on the Hot 100 in 1980. They had two more mid-level chart hits in 1981 with “Love Is Like a Rock” and “My Girl.”



	His modest success during that era on the Billboard charts was hardly indicative of just how beloved he was in his native Pennsylvania and the Midwest region, widely seen as being to Pittsburgh what Michael Stanley was to Cleveland.

	“For my money, he was the most beloved Pittsburgh musician of all time,” Joe Grushecky told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette. Grushecky, as the leader of the Iron City Houserockers, would have been one of the few other viable candidates for that title. But, as he told the newspaper, “I don’t know anyone who was loved more than Donnie. He just had that warmth about him, and it came through in his performance.”

	Iris was a trouper to the end, performing his final show less than a month ago, on Sept. 28, at Citizens Live at the Wylie, seated in a chair shortly after having radiation treatment in the afternoon.


	“He sang like a bird that night,” his longtime keyboard player and best friend, Mark Avsec, told the Post-Gazette. “It was the first time on a chair, and he didn’t like that. But the poor guy, the cancer was spreading, and he was in pain, and he really wanted to do that show and be with the people.”

	Iris began singing in a doo-wop group in high school in the early ’60s, then moved on to rock ‘n’ roll and R&B cover bands before the Jaggerz were formed in 1964. They were eventually signed to Gamble Records, the brainchild of Philly soul greats Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, and released their first album, “Introducing the Jaggerz,” in 1969.


	In the late ’70s, he became a guitarist for Wild Cherry, after that group had already hit the big time with “Play That Funky Music.” It was in the Wild Cherry days that he met Avsec, who continued on with him in Donnie Iris and the Cruisers and continued to perform with him all the way to last month.
	

	They recruited Marty Lee Hoenes, Albritton McClain and Kevin Valentine to complete Donnie and the Cruisers and released their first album, “Back on the Streets,” in 1980, followed by “King Cool” the following year, “The High and the Mighty” in 1982 and “Fortune 410” in 1983 before being dropped by MCA Records in 1984. Even set adrift from major labels, they continued to record into the 2010s.



	Iris was championed in 2025 in a well-read blog post by industry pundit Bob Lefsetz, who wrote, “I didn’t buy the solo debut, ‘Back on the Streets,’ but I did buy the follow-up, ‘King Cool.’ The joke, of course, was that Donnie Iris was anything but cool. He was a man whose music was au courant, but whose look was passé, maybe because by time he made it he was in his late thirties, whereas his contemporaries had all made it in their twenties…”

	Lefsetz continued, “Donnie specializes in straight-ahead rock, and all his records are very listenable. So I did, listen that is. I know ‘Stagedoor Johnny’ and ‘Never Did I’ by heart, not that you can hear them on streaming services, MCA has only deigned to release the greatest hits. And then Donnie Iris lost his deal with MCA and disappeared. ‘Ah! Leah!’ survived, some people remember seeing him on MTV, but there was no press, no airplay, it’s like he didn’t exist.”
	

	Then, as Lefsetz noted, “Turns out he became a mortgage broker… Sure, Donnie continued to play music, but he needed to pay the rent, put food on the table. You’d be stunned so many of your heroes end up working straight jobs.” 

	Indeed, per the Post-Gazette, Iris went on to own SimCorp in Aliquippa. He admitted he got some business from customers who wanted to deal with the rock star they’d identified with or grown up with, or whose annual birthday shows they were still going to see. “It got me some business I normally wouldn’t have,” he acknowledged.


	Lefsetz was compelled to write about iris by seeing a video of him performing “Love Is Like a Rock” and, like many fans, being impressed he still had his chops, “sans plastic surgery, sans much hair. It’s still him, the essence… What is truly stunning is when he starts picking that Fender. Like it’s a high school in New Castle, Pennsylvania and it’s another night in the sixties. And he’s not only picking, HE’S INTO IT!… Donnie isn’t showing off, he’s just doing what he does, AT 82! It put a smile on my face, made me feel good not only about Donnie Iris, but rock and roll.”

	In one of dozens of responses to Lefsetz’s column, his partner Avsec wrote, “We’ve been together for almost 50 years… And one of the joys of my life is watching the crowd watch Donnie. I’ve never seen such JOY on people’s faces. It happens every time we play, and we’re fortunate enough to be playing decent size venues, especially in Western Pa and Northeastern Ohio. Donnie is going through his third course of chemotherapy. If the treatments drag him down, he does not show it. He still sings his butt off. Screams and everything. I don’t think he has ever had so much fun on stage. Donnie always tells me he’s having the time of his life. Same goes for me.”

	In another response, former A&M promo executive Richard Pachter wrote, “‘Ah! Leah!’ may be the most rock and roll video ever made. That rug! Those teeth! That skinny guy with the hairy chest! But despite all that, it’s beyond great. It’s the personification of it all. I’m not kidding! THAT is rock and roll!”

schema.headline: Donnie Iris, Pittsburgh’s Favorite Rocker, Who Scored Hits With the Jaggerz and as a Solo Artist, Dies at 83

title: Jon Stewart Trolls Trump’s Nicki Minaj Fixation After ‘Beautiful Ass’ Comment: ‘He’s Like Yogi Bear Floating Towards a Pie’
description: On Monday night’s episode of “The Daily Show,” Jon Stewart trolled Donald Trump’s fixation on Nicki Minaj as the president’s odd remarks about the
body:
On Monday night’s episode of “The Daily Show,” Jon Stewart trolled Donald Trump’s fixation on Nicki Minaj as the president’s odd remarks about the rapper’s “beautiful ass” have been making the rounds across the internet.

	Stewart began the evening’s show by focusing on the midterm elections, and the issues that voters are, “for some reason,” fixated on: the economy, cost of living and the war in Iran. “Donald Trump is actually back out there on the campaign trail to make his closing arguments. I imagine the president will be laser-focused on the issues that matter most,” said Stewart before cutting to a clip of Trump saying: “I looked at his ass, and I’ve never done that with a man before. A man’s ass, his ass, the ass. His ass was like a big piece of muscle.”
	

	“And by the way, don’t feel left out, ladies. Trump’s got plenty of ammo left for you,” he continued, before cutting to a clip of the president during Saturday’s rally in Michigan showing him saying, “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before — Nicki Minaj. That’s hard to miss.”

	Stewart, bewildered, said, “How the fuck is this real? ‘Stand up, Nikki. Twirl around. Give us a look at that.’ Talk about inflation, my God!” He continued: “Look at Trump’s face when Minaj is talking. Look at what he’s doing. He’s transfixed. He’s staring at her ass. He’s like Yogi Bear floating towards a pie on a windowsill.”

	Stewart also took aim at an ad from Ohio Republican governor hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy that features Democratic candidate Amy Acton’s estranged mother.
	

	“Well, that could be a compelling ad if it weren’t for just a couple of mitigating factors,” said Stewart. “For instance, Acton’s mother hasn’t spoken to her daughter in 50 years, and the reason is, oh, cartoonishly evil word generator, she lost custody of her kids because her husband at the time was indicted for raping her daughter.”

	Stewart then cut to a clip of Trump defending the ad, and calling the reporter asking him if “the sexual abuse allegations mean nothing to” him a “horrible little reporter.” Stewart then asked: “When did Donald Trump become Miss Hannigan?”

	Ahead of last week’s show, it was announced that Stewart would remain the host of “The Daily Show” through 2028. Stewart’s contract was set to end at the end of 2026 after signing a one-year renewal in November 2025. Stewart made his hosting debut on “The Daily Show” in 1999, left in 2015, and returned in February 2024. After his return, “The Daily Show” ratings went up.

	Check out the entire monologue below.

title: Jay-Z to Perform at Apple Music 2027 Super Bowl Halftime Show
description: Jay-Z is slated to perform at the Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show, taking place on Feb. 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California
body:
Jay-Z is slated to perform at the Apple Music Super Bowl LXI Halftime Show, taking place on Feb. 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

	“From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey,” said Jay-Z in a statement. “Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world’s biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true.”


	The announcement comes on the heels of an anniversary victory lap this year under the banner “Jay-Z 30.” He kicked off the celebrations as a headliner at the Roots Picnic in late May, followed by three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium in July to honor the 25th and 30th anniversaries of his albums “The Blueprint” and “Reasonable Doubt,” respectively. In addition to international shows in Paris and London, Jay sat down with Rick Rubin for the eight-part docuseries “Jay-Z in 8” where he broke down hits and deep cuts across his catalog. This past weekend, he brought his global string of tour dates to a close at SoFi Stadium with two nights featuring guest appearances from Scarface, DJ Khaled, John Legend, Blue Ivy Carter, Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too Short.
	



	“For several years, we’ve had the privilege of working closely with Jay-Z and Roc Nation, and I’ve seen the extraordinary impact he has had on the Super Bowl Halftime Show,” said NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell in a statement. “When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that Jay-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him. I couldn’t be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage.”
	

	“Jay-Z’s impact on global music culture is as profound as it is undeniable,” added Oliver Schusser, Apple’s Vice President of Music and International Content. “We’ve had the privilege of working closely with him these last few years to bring some of the world’s most exciting and prolific artists to the Super Bowl Halftime Show stage and we are so thrilled that he will be taking that stage himself this year. We know it’s going to be an incredible show.”

	The Super Bowl Halftime Show will air on ESPN, ABC and Disney+, and on mobile devices with NFL+. ESPN’s Spanish-language telecast will also be available on ESPN Deportes and Disney+, with a separate Spanish-language presentation on Univision. Roc Nation will executive produce the show, while Hamish Hamilton will serve as director.



	

	



	Earlier this year, Bad Bunny held court as the Super Bowl Halftime Show performer, celebrating his Puerto Rican heritage in the tradition of Latin America. The elaborate set included a mock sugar-cane field and a Puerto Rican vecindad with a barber shop, liquor store and a casita where Bad Bunny welcomed celebrity guests including Jessica Alba, Karol G, Cardi B, Young Miko and Pedro Pascal, among others. Bad Bunny also brought out surprise artists Lady Gaga and Ricky Martin for a salsa-inflected version of “Die With a Smile” and “lo que le pasó a Hawái,” respectively.

	The Benito Bowl, as it was affectionately dubbed by his fans, reached an average of 128.2 million viewers, above the 124.9 million average viewers achieved by the Super Bowl overall but down from the 133.5 million viewers reached by Kendrick Lamar in 2025. Before Lamar, Usher held the record for most viewers with his 2024 performance.

	Last month, Bad Bunny won his first Emmy for his Super Bowl Halftime Show performance in the outstanding special (live) category. The spectacle took home a total of seven wins, including musical direction, choreography, sound mixing, lighting design, technical direction/camerawork and directing.

	Speaking about the performance, creative director Harriet Cuddeford previously told Variety, “The performance is celebrating normal people, and what it is to be human and love and have joy, and really appreciate one another. This was to show how much he values his community, to celebrate normal people on the world’s biggest stage, especially people who are of importance in Latino culture. He’s a very authentic person, Benito, and it’s about just being authentic and very real and very human.”
	

	In addition to the aforementioned artists, recent performers at the Super Bowl Halftime Show have included Rihanna, the Weeknd and a collective performance from Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg, Eminem, Mary J. Blige, Lamar, 50 Cent and Anderson .Paak.

title: Taylor Swift, Inducted Into Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, Says ‘There Is No Music Community Like This Music Community. I Know, I Checked All the Communities’
description: Taylor Swift looked back on her earliest days crafting songs in Music City as she was inducted Monday  into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame,
body:
Taylor Swift looked back on her earliest days crafting songs in Music City as she was inducted Monday  into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, becoming its youngest member at 36. Swift was inducted by former tourmate Brad Paisley, whom she teased, and serenaded by Lainey Wilson, whom she praised, before launching into a lengthy speech about what she learned in the trenches of Music Row as a teenager.

	“I was lucky enough to get a publishing deal with Sony Publishing when I was 14, and I just hit the ground running,” she told the audience at the Music City Center ceremony. “I was like a sponge, and I had really curly hair and it was yellow, so I kind of looked like a sponge, too,” she quipped.
	

	Praising the town that she said raised her, Swift said, “There is no music community like this music community. I know. I checked all the communities.”



	

					(L-R) Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller, Taylor Swift, George Strait and Bruce Channel attend the 56th Nashville Songwriters Hall Of Fame Gala at Music City Center on October 26, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TAS)
									Ed Rode
	



	Swift was being inducted alongside Lyle Lovett, Bruce Channel, Shawn Camp and Lee Thomas Miller (plus the late J.I. Allison, of Buddy Holly and the Crickets). Also being honored with a special award at the ceremony was country superstar George Strait, who was getting the Career Maker Award, something only one other artist has received, in honor of what he has accomplished for others performing their material.

	The tradition at Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame ceremonies is for the inductees not to sing or play themselves but rather to enjoy a performance of one of their songs by another notable star or major figure. In this case it was Lainey Wilson doing a stripped-back version of “Love Story,” to which Swift offered some reciprocal support by getting in a plug for Wilson’s new single.
	



	“You know, I first of all want to say thank you to Lainey Wilson, who I just think is one of the coolest people in the world,” Swift said, “for saying yes and doing that. And I’ve had her new single on repeat. It just puts me in the best mood. It’s called ‘Kinda Love It.’ Check it out.”

	Paisley gave an introduction in which he recalled marveling at how she went from proving she was a star with her first two albums and proving once and for all that she was a songwriting all-timer with her entirely self-penned third album. “All of us were like, ‘How is this teenager doing this? How is she so brilliant?’ And then she goes off and really put her feelings into something that is 100% hers and writes the ‘Speak Now’ album all by herself,” he reminisced. “It’s an amazing thing to watch her evolution from somebody who realized this all starts with a song to (being able to) take that exact thing and change the world with it.”

	In turn, Swift turned the laudatory mood more light-hearted as she recalled the days when she opened for Paisley on a summer amphitheater tour between her first and second albums. He and his band and his opening acts would always famously play prans on each other, and Swift suggested it might have gone a bit too next-level by the end.

	“Brad Paisley, thank you so much for that induction. I’m really surprised to see you here, actually,” she said, “because we’ve been estranged since 2007. I think you know why. Crickets. He took a tour prank too far. Filled my entire tour bus with live crickets. Thousands of them. Oh my God. For months, I couldn’t sleep. Just chirp… chirp… chirp.” A pause, and then, again: “Chirp — all night. I considered buying a pet lizard to eradicate the problem. It was a dark time. But you know what? You did such an amazing job with that introduction, I think we can let bygones be bygones. Thank you. Yeah, I think we’re good now.”

	Getting into the serious grist of her speech, Swift focused on the three words that make up the primary name of her honor — “Nashville,” “Songwriters” and “Fame” — and devoted individual time to each of them.

	She said that even as a young child, songwriting was “what I centered my entire life around,” and Nashville became “the place that I went to in my middle school daydreams. It was the place where all the wisdom that I wished to acquire existed in one place. … And it ended up being all of that and more. It ended up being everything.”
	



	

					Taylor Swift attends the 56th Nashville Songwriters Hall Of Fame Gala at Music City Center on October 26, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee.  (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TAS)
									Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TAS
	



	As for the fame part, Swift described that as almost incidental, yet also almost all-consuming, as “a byproduct of my love for music. … It’s why a lot of people know the words to my music, which is awesome. It’s also why there’s these daily random doses of chaos that just pop up in my life every once in a while — every couple of hours. That can be weird, but I have tools in place in my mind that help me navigate that and get back to true north when life feels so bizarre. Those tools are my memories,” and she suggested that “the memories that I visit most frequently when I need to return back to some semblance of remembering what normalcy is and why I do this” are from her early years in Nashville.

	Swift credited songwriting sessions as a kid as places where she “learned which ideas are worth fighting for (and) which ideas are worth letting go of… I learned how to accommodate when your co-writer has a hangover, or when they’re going to need to talk about their divorce for a really long time before we write anything. One thing that I did learn is that songwriters, although they possess the superhuman ability to understand and interpret the human condition and have insane levels of empathy — they re just people too. And they are people who in a lot of ways raised me and guided me through my formative years.”




	Swift did a bit of name-dropping, like how she got to know not just Catherine, the woman who worked the front desk at the Jody Williams Music publishing company, but her boyfriend and future husband, Eric Church. She mentioned running up the stairs to the writing room to meet up with frequent collaborator Liz Rose, where she would say, “Liz, this happened at school today…” And then she would run to the garden shed behind the building that was the one-person studio for Nathan Chapman, who played every instrument on her demos and “interpreted my music so intuitively that later on I would fight for him to produce my entire first album. It was our first album, for both of us. And I am shocked and stunned to say that as of a couple days ago, that album is 20 years old.”
	

	In summary, Swift said, “It’s not lost on me how crazy this is. I will cherish it forever because Nashville is the place that honed and polished the thing about myself and the thing about my life that I am the most proud of and the most passionate about… It just feels like one of those amazing Nashville moments I’m going to revisit on a rainy day.”

	Swift, who was wearing a burgundy floral Raina Vanessa minidress to the ceremony, was getting the honor just four months after she received a similar accolade. She was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in New York in June; she was also the youngest writer to receive that honor.

	Among other presentations during the evening, the late J.I. Allison was inducted by music journalist/author/historian Robert K. Oermann, followed by BR5-49 frontman Chuck Mead performing the Crickets classic “That’ll Be The Day.” Joanie Allison accepted on her husband’s behalf.

	Bruce Channel had Kix Brooks of Brooks & Dunn as his presenter, followed by Lee Roy Parnell performing “Hey! Baby!”

	Lyle Lovett was celebrated with Hall of Fame songwriter Alger presenting and Kathy Mattea doing the performance honors with “If I Had A Boat.”

	Shawn Camp got his honors via Emmylou Harris and songwriter Verlon Thompson performing “Magnolia Wind,” preceded by a presentation from Jim Lauderdale.

	The night was rounded out by Jamey Johnson saluting Lee Thomas Miller with the hit they co-wrote, “In Color.” Alabama’s Randy Owen did Miller’s presentation.

	The show also featured a tribute to the late Bill Cody, the longtime WSM radio personality and Opry emcee who had been the announcer for the Songwriters Hall of Fame gala for years. Hall of Fame member Rivers Rutherford performed his co-written “When I Get Where I’m Going” in salute to Cody and all the Hall of Fame members who died in the preceding year — Dolly Parton, John Anderson, Walt Aldridge, Rory Bourke, Steve Cropper, Jim McBride, Joe Melson and Don Schlitz.

title: Searchlight Pictures Marketing EVP Michelle Hooper Exits Studio
description:
Michelle Hooper is leaving Searchlight Pictures as executive vice president of marketing after two decades with the company.

	Since joining in 200
body:
Michelle Hooper is leaving Searchlight Pictures as executive vice president of marketing after two decades with the company.

	Since joining in 2006, Hooper’s work on publicity, awards and creative marketing helped earn the studio nearly 200 Oscar nominations and more than 130 Golden Globe nominations. Of those 200, Searchlight took home 49 wins, including best picture winners “Nomadland,” “The Shape of Water,” “Birdman,” “12 Years a Slave” and “Slumdog Millionaire.” Searchlight also received best picture nominations at the Golden Globes for the aforementioned titles, in addition to 15 others.
	

	This awards season, Hooper was leading campaigns for “Wild Horse Nine” and “Behemonth!,” among other titles.

	“She’s a stellar leader for her creative insights and keen ability to read a film for where it fits in the zeitgeist, in turn setting her team up for wide-reaching success,” said a longtime colleague. “But she’s also an equally formidable collaborator, one who can close a campaign with all the insights gained from keeping her ear to the ground and hearing feedback in real time. It’s a loss for the studio, but I guarantee you it will be another’s gain.”

	Earlier in her career, Hooper worked at CBS Entertainment as the director of entertainment communications and aided in the “Survivor” publicity strategy; she also spent four years at Fox Broadcast as the company’s VP of entertainment publicity, where she worked on campaigns for shows like “The Simpsons,” “Arrested Development” and “American Idol.”
	

	Hooper was featured in Variety’s 2025 Women’s Impact Report alongside fellow Searchlight executives Rebecca Kearey, DanTram Nguyen and Katie Goodson-Thomas, whose work to ensure the studio had a stellar year at the Oscars was highlighted.

	“The team’s marketing mojo led to 10 Academy Award nominations for ‘A Complete Unknown’ and ‘A Real Pain,’ including a best supporting actor win for Kieran Culkin’s performance in the Jesse Eisenberg film,” wrote Variety.

	In a joint statement, the team explained that Searchlight’s adventurous choices and deep filmmaker relationships help the company weather the challenges of the business by “trusting [that] audiences still want films that entertain, challenge and provoke.”

                          Says He's ‘Drowning Financially,’ Struggling to Pay Bills
                          Following Drastic Income Drop After Losing Fox Sports Pay
                      
                  
                                                                        Published

                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Paul Pierce claims he is "tapped out" financially while trying to keep up with his court-ordered support payments ... due to him no longer receiving income from Fox Sports ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, Paul claims his last check from Fox Sports came in August. He said his average monthly income was $119K, but now it is zero. He said he earned around $23K last month from his partnership interests in other business ventures.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Paul said he pays around $28K in child support and another $20K in spousal support per month … but claims he only has $300K in the bank and $3 million in property.
      

            He says he spends around $48K a month in bills, including $8K in childcare, $5K in groceries, $7K on eating out, $3,200 on utilities, $1K on clothes, $3,500 on entertainment, and various other expenses.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Paul is asking the court to shut down his ex-wife Princess Santiago’s request for $40K in legal fees and another $10K for a forensic accountant. She claimed Paul was playing games about his financial records ... and wanted an expert to review his finances.
      
    
            In his filing, Paul's attorney said Paul would have "great difficulty" paying these fees since his Fox Sports contract was terminated ... adding that he was "drowning financially" and having trouble keeping up with the monetary obligations
      
    
            Princess’ request for additional funds came after Paul was ordered to pay Princess $8,508 per month in temporary child support for their son, King. He was also ordered to pay $100K in legal fees.
      
    
            Paul reportedly earned around $200 million during his NBA career.
